claims.text: A coherent dispersion of nanometric yttria particles enhances the high-temperature yield strength of tungsten-based alloys.
A coherent dispersion of nanometric yttria particles enhances the high-temperature toughness of tungsten-based alloys.
Nanometric yttria particles pin dislocations in tungsten.
Nanometric yttria particles inhibit grain-boundary sliding in tungsten.
Nanometric yttria particles inhibit thermally activated dislocation climb in tungsten.
A 1–2 vol% nanometric yttria dispersion can be introduced into tungsten through mechanical alloying and powder metallurgy while matching grain size and thermal history to an unmodified baseline.
The relevant yttria particles are uniformly distributed both at grain boundaries and within tungsten grains.
High-temperature plastic strain in tungsten primarily results from thermally activated dislocation climb.
High-temperature plastic strain in tungsten primarily results from grain-boundary sliding.
Yttria particles stabilize dislocation networks in tungsten at high temperature.
Yttria-induced inhibition of dislocation mobility delays the onset of extensive plastic deformation.
Yttria-induced inhibition of dislocation mobility enhances strain hardening.
Enhanced strain hardening contributes to greater toughness in ODS tungsten.
ODS tungsten will have higher yield strength than grain-structure- and thermal-history-matched unmodified tungsten at 800–1200°C.
ODS tungsten will have greater toughness than the matched unmodified tungsten baseline at 800–1200°C.
ODS tungsten will exhibit a more stable, pinned dislocation network than the unmodified tungsten baseline.
ODS tungsten will exhibit less microstructural evidence of grain-boundary sliding than the unmodified tungsten baseline.
The proposed mechanism should apply in inert or high-vacuum environments between 800°C and 1200°C when microstructural features other than the nanoparticle dispersion are held consistent.
The stated 800–1200°C inert or high-vacuum conditions are typical of fusion plasma-facing component conditions.
Uncontrolled microstructural differences between ODS and baseline samples may alter dislocation dynamics and confound the comparison.
